newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea reforms may spur long-term bond market.
newsitem.headline: South Korea reforms may spur long-term bond market.

text.p: South Korea's bid to boost private-sector investment in infrastructure projects by allowing investors to issue long-term bonds could spur the growth of a long-term debt market, bond traders said on Monday.

Private developers are to be allowed to issue bonds with a maturity of more than 12 years in early 1997, the Ministry of Finance and Economy said. Detailed terms and pricing of the bonds will be determined later.
The ministry said it had decided to allow private companies to issue long-term bonds due to the lengthy debt period an infrastructure project needs for completion.
Bond dealers applauded the government's decision to raise funds through bonds given that it would help activate South Korea's almost non-existent long-term debt market.
"The move will contribute to the growth of the South Korean bond market by activating long-term bond trading," said Woo Chung-hee, a bond dealer at Hanwha Securities.
"Currently the market is less accomodative to those who want to raise funds for long-term investment because most debt instruments are short term," said Woo.
Presently the South Korean debt market is dominated by bonds with maturities of five years or less. These bonds accounted for 94 percent of total bond issues in 1995.
Bond dealers said it would take time for "the long-term infrastructure bonds" to gain popularity.

"The long-term bonds may not attract buyers immediately," said a bond trader at Daewoo Securities. "Korea's institutional and individual investors are not accustomed to bonds with maturity over 12 years."
Dealers said the market participants would look carefully at new issues when they were introduced early next year.
"It will take investors three to six months to familiarise themselves with the new bonds," said Woo of Hanwha. "They'll check to see if it's a safe instrument to invest in."
He said the government should publicise the new long-term bonds long ahead of the first issue, giving details to put investors at ease.
The government should also make sure that there was liquidity for the long-term bonds in the secondary market, dealers said.

"To ensure liquidity in the secondary market, there has to be a merit for the long-term bonds buyers," said Kang Yung-gee, bond dealer at Hyundai Securities. "If the market's not going to be liquid, investors will lose interest."
Dealers said rather than issuing a variety of different bonds, issuing organisations should stick to one type of bond to guarantee more liquidity in the secondary market.
Separately, the ministry also said it would expand loans for private-sector infrastructure developers.
Private firms participating in a project worth 500 billion won ($606 million) or more would be allowed to borrow from the state-run Korea Development Bank.
Currently, companies involved in projects worth one trillion won or more are allowed to borrow from the bank.
